assessment.nobel_worthiness: Strategic bargaining with alternating offers is a foundational result in game theory. It underpins models of negotiation, search and decentralized markets, and has shaped applied theory in labour, industrial organisation and monetary economics. The conceptual contribution is deep, and the field has long digested it.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein's 1982 alternating-offers model is the core contribution. Rubinstein and Wolinsky's work on bargaining in markets extends it to decentralized trade. Binmore's work on the Nash programme and on the strategic foundations of bargaining is important and complementary, but it is the weaker claim on the central result. Ståhl's earlier finite-horizon work is a further attribution complication.
assessment.maturity: Very mature. The core results date from 1982 to 1990, and the field has had decades to confirm their influence. The main risk is that recognition is long overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer a broader game-theory or bargaining prize that includes Binmore.
Rubinstein's contribution is largely a single-author result, so a one- or two-person prize is possible.
Some members may view the topic as covered by earlier game-theory and mechanism-design prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Measuring intergenerational mobility with population-scale administrative data changed how economists and policymakers study opportunity. It combines credible quasi-experimental design with large-scale data and has direct policy relevance on neighbourhood effects and tax-record-based measurement.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure in both the measurement and the research programme. Hendren is credited for the causal neighbourhood-effects work. Friedman is credited for the data infrastructure and the tax-record studies. Katz's role in the Moving to Opportunity analysis is real, but the three-person limit forces a choice, and this selection is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature, with major results from about 2014 to 2022. Replication and external validation have been extensive, though some long-run causal claims are still debated.
uncertainties: Choice among Friedman, Katz and others for the third slot.
Chetty also appears in other candidate areas, so the credit is spread across several lines of work.
Open debate on causal interpretation of neighbourhood effects and on measurement sensitivity.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work established empirically how trade exposure and technology reshape local labour markets and wage inequality. It also changed trade policy debates and the understanding of adjustment costs. The influence on labour, trade and political economy is wide.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock research is the work of Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The earlier task-based and skill-bias framework involves Katz and others, and the wider technology-and-labour-demand literature has other major contributors who are not on this ballot entry. The cleanest and most coherent trio is Autor, Dorn and Hanson.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Core papers date from about 2003 to 2016, with extensive follow-up. Some interpretation of the long-run effects continues to be debated.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with other labour and technology prize candidates.
Debate over magnitudes and external validity of the China-shock estimates.
The candidate combines two programmes (tasks and trade shocks), which complicates the coherence of a single prize rationale.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design are a conceptually clean theoretical framework. They unify and generalize the study of strategic information transmission, with applications to markets, regulation, auctions and platform design. The theoretical depth is high and the framework is widely used.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica and Gentzkow's 2011 paper introduced the persuasion model. Bergemann and Morris developed the information-design and robust-predictions programme, which is closely related but distinct. Morris is the strongest bridge between the two lines, but the team structure is a real attribution question.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. The foundational work dates from about 2011 to 2019, and the applied impact is still growing. Time may increase confidence about lasting influence.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would reward the theory this soon after its development.
Choice between Morris and Bergemann for the third slot.
Gentzkow's other empirical contributions are outside this candidate's scope.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models changed the analysis of monetary and fiscal transmission by putting household balance sheets, marginal propensities to consume and distribution at the centre of macro models. The framework is now a standard tool in central banks and academia.
assessment.attribution: The 2018 Kaplan–Moll–Violante paper is the defining contribution, and the trio is a natural and coherent grouping. Earlier incomplete-markets foundations (Aiyagari, Huggett, Krusell–Smith and others) are important antecedents, which complicates how much credit belongs to this group.
assessment.maturity: Relatively young, with most results from about 2014 to 2024. Policy and empirical validation are ongoing, so a prize now would be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Whether the field has fully settled on the framework's empirical performance.
Credit relative to the incomplete-markets antecedents.
Timing: later recognition may be more likely.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The structural estimation of demand and dynamic industry models made it possible to measure market power, welfare and merger effects with realistic differentiated-product data. The methods are standard in industrial organisation, antitrust and regulation practice.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (BLP) are the core of the demand-estimation approach, and Pakes is central to the dynamic-model line (Ericson–Pakes and related work). Bresnahan, Reiss and others made key contributions to empirical industrial organisation that this selection does not credit.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with core work from about 1994 to 2000 and decades of use in practice.
uncertainties: Many strong contributors, so the three-person limit leaves out important names (Bresnahan, Reiss, Berry–Haile and others).
Whether the committee sees this as a methodological or an applied prize.
Dynamic-model estimation has had mixed practical adoption.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Melitz (2003) model of firm heterogeneity and selection reoriented trade theory around firms. It changed the understanding of gains from trade, and it also reshaped empirical work on exporters and productivity. The influence on theory and measurement is broad.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the clear originator of the core model. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple extended it, and Redding's contributions on quantitative trade and spatial models are related but belong to a different line. A single-laureate proposal is the cleanest expression of the core discovery, though a prize might be shared with other trade theorists.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The key paper is from 2003, and the empirical and quantitative follow-up is extensive.
uncertainties: A single-name proposal may be too narrow if the committee wants to recognise the wider new-trade-theory line.
Overlap with other trade candidates on the list.
Some members may prefer to wait for a broader trade prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantile regression is a widely used econometric tool for analysing distributional effects beyond the mean. It has become a standard method in labour economics, finance and applied statistics, and its practical reach across fields is very large.
assessment.attribution: Koenker and Bassett's 1978 paper introduced the estimator, and Koenker's subsequent work developed theory, computation and applications. Chernozhukov's contributions (inference, instrumental quantile regression) are important but belong more to a later extension, and he also appears on other candidate entries.
assessment.maturity: Very mature. The method has had more than four decades of confirmation and use.
uncertainties: Committee preference between a methods prize and a discovery prize.
Quantile-type ideas have antecedents in the statistics literature.
Competition from other econometrics candidates with possibly wider conceptual impact.
